title: The role of fungi in soil health
seoTitle: The role of fungi in soil health
subtitle: Mycorrhizae, decomposers and pathogen antagonists strengthen crop fertility and resilience
excerpt: Fungi are essential soil partners: they connect roots to nutrients, recycle organic matter and protect plants from diseases, ensuring productivity.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Invisible fungi work beneath our feet, turning soil into a living and resilient environment. Their activity goes far beyond decomposition, directly influencing agricultural productivity.

Fungi as soil engineers

Unlike organisms that simply occupy space, fungi alter the physical structure of soil. By producing filamentous structures called hyphae, they create networks that bind mineral particles, increasing porosity and facilitating water retention. This modification improves aeration and reduces compaction, allowing roots to penetrate more easily and absorb resources more efficiently.

Mycorrhizae: the bridge between roots and nutrients

One of the most studied relationships between fungi and plants occurs in mycorrhizae, symbiotic associations in which fungi exchange nutrients with roots. While the plant supplies carbon in the form of sugars, the fungus extends its mycelium far beyond the root zone, capturing phosphorus, nitrogen and micronutrients that would otherwise be inaccessible. This exchange can increase phosphorus availability up to tenfold, a crucial element for root development and flowering.

Benefits for productivity

Plants that establish mycorrhizae exhibit greater vigor, higher drought resistance and lower need for chemical fertilizers. In small-scale cropping systems, farmers observe more uniform harvests and fewer losses during periods of water stress.

Invisible decomposers: organic matter recycling

Saprotrophic fungi play the role of recyclers by breaking down dead organic matter such as leaves, roots and crop residues. During this process they convert complex compounds into simple forms that can be reused by beneficial microorganisms and by the plants themselves. Controlled decomposition prevents the buildup of organic material that could attract pests, while enriching the soil with humus, a substance that improves cation exchange capacity.

Interaction with soil bacteria

The material released by fungi serves as food for nitrifying bacteria, which transform ammonia into nitrate, a form of nitrogen readily absorbable by plants. This synergy between fungi and bacteria creates a continuous nutrient cycle, reducing dependence on external inputs.

Fungi in pathogen suppression and plant promotion

Some fungi act as natural antagonists of organisms that cause crop diseases. They compete for space and resources, produce antibiotic compounds and even induce defense responses in host plants. This biological protection lowers the incidence of diseases such as fusarium and powdery mildew, reducing the need for synthetic fungicides.

Induction of systemic resistance

When a plant comes into contact with certain beneficial fungi, it can activate defense mechanisms that make it less susceptible to future attacks. This phenomenon, known as induced systemic resistance, adds an extra layer of safety for the crop at no additional cost.

Practical applications for Brazilian farmers

Incorporating the benefits of fungi into crop management can be done simply and economically. Practices such as crop rotation, maintaining vegetative cover and applying mycorrhizal inoculants increase the population of beneficial fungi. Moreover, using organic residues as compost or green manure provides food for the mycelium, boosting soil biological activity.

For those seeking to reduce chemical inputs, a direct-seeding strategy followed by inoculation with specific fungi represents a viable alternative. This practice improves germination, increases emergence uniformity and favors early root establishment.

In regions where soil erosion is a recurring problem, introducing fungi that produce exopolysaccharides helps form stable aggregates, mitigating loss of fertile soil. Thus, farmers can preserve the arable layer and ensure long-term production continuity.

Understanding the role of fungi in soil health transforms how agriculture is conducted. By recognizing these microorganisms as strategic allies, it is possible to build more resilient, less input-dependent productive systems that can sustain the country’s food security.
